'''Malvin Avram Ruderman''' (March 25, 1927 – July 20, 2024) was an American physicist and astrophysicist.

==Education==
Mal Ruderman received his A.B. degree from [[Columbia University]] in 1945.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Columbia College (Columbia University). Office of Alumni Affairs and Development |url=http://archive.org/details/ldpd_12981092_019 |title=Columbia College today |last2=Columbia College (Columbia University) |date=1974–1977 |publisher=New York, New York. : Columbia College, Office of Alumni Affairs and Development |others=Columbia University Libraries}}</ref> His MS degree (1947) and PhD (1951) are from the [[California Institute of Technology]] under the supervision of [[Robert Jay Finkelstein]].<ref name='aip'>American Institute of Physics, Physics History Network, [https://history.aip.org/phn/11601018.html "Malvin A. Ruderman"]</ref><ref>Mathematics Genealogy Project, [https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=175970 "Malvin Ruderman"]</ref>

==Career==
In 1951–53, Ruderman worked at Berkeley's [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory|Radiation Laboratory]]. He became an assistant professor at UC Berkeley in 1953, rising by 1964 to the rank of full professor.  He moved to [[New York University]] in 1964, and to Columbia University in 1969, becoming Centennial Professor in 1980.  Ruderman served as chair of the Department of Physics at Columbia in 1973–75.<ref name='aip' />

With [[Charles Kittel]] in 1954, Ruderman discovered the [[RKKY interaction]] for nuclear magnetic moments in certain metals (independently developed by Kasuya and Yosida, hence its name). His later research interests in astrophysics include collapsed objects in astrophysics, neutron stars, and gamma ray emission.<ref name='aip' />

In the early 1960s, Ruderman was a member of the committee that conceived the [[Berkeley Physics Course]].  He developed the first draft of the first volume, ''Mechanics'', for use at Berkeley in 1963. With Charles Kittel and [[Walter D. Knight]], he was co-author of the final published volume.<ref>Charles Kittel, Walter D. Knight, and Malvin Ruderman, ''Mechanics: Berkeley Course in Physics, Volume 1'', McGraw-Hill (1965), Preface, p. ix.</ref>

In 1969, Ruderman and (independently) [[Gordon Baym]], [[Christopher Pethick]], and [[David Pines]], were the first to propose that discontinuous slowings observed in [[neutron star]]s, so called [[Starquake (astrophysics)|starquakes]], were due to the cracking of the star's solid crust, under increasing stress due to the gradual slowdown of the [[pulsar]].<ref>Malcolm S. Longair, The Cosmic Century: A History of Astrophysics and Cosmology, Cambridge University Press (2006), p. 196.</ref> Ruderman died on July 20, 2024, at the age of 97.<ref>{{Cite news |date=20 July 2024 |title=Malvin Ruderman obituary |url=https://fas.columbia.edu/news/memoriam-professor-mal-ruderman |access-date=20 November 2024}}</ref>

==Honors==
Ruderman was awarded a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] in 1956.  He was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1972,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Malvin A. Ruderman|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/malvin-a-ruderman-5ql68a/|access-date=2021-12-13|website=nasonline.org}}</ref> the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1974,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Malvin Avram Ruderman|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/malvin-avram-ruderman|access-date=2021-12-13|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|language=en}}</ref> and the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 1996.<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Malvin+A.+Ruderman&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=2021-12-13|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> He is a recipient of the Pregel Medal of the [[New York Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/malvin-ruderman |title=Malvin Ruderman - Scholars &#124; Institute for Advanced Study |date=December 9, 2019 }}</ref>
